home.hero: A graph tracing 168 mechanics across 618 games and 394 companies, from Spacewar! in 1962 to the present, showing which ideas descended from which.
home.sub: Pick any mechanic — regenerating health, the battle pass, lock-on targeting — and pull its thread backward to the game that first shipped it and forward to everything built on top of it. Three lenses sit over the same timeline: the feature ontology, franchise descent from sequel to sequel, and the studio lineage of who spun out of, acquired, or renamed whom.

sections.p: Genre sorts games by what they resemble. An ontology sorts them by what they are made of: 168 named mechanics, each with a family, a first appearance, and a list of the earlier mechanics it revises. Constrained Weapon Loadout is a Halo argument about hit points. Defense of the Ancients is a Warcraft III map arguing simultaneously with Dune II's production loop and EverQuest's cooldowns. Sorted this way, a fighting game and a soulslike turn out to share a defensive verb, and the seasonal battle pass turns out to descend, through Call of Duty 4's prestige ranks, from the initials Asteroids kept in battery-backed RAM.

Time runs left to right, 1958 to 2026. In the feature lens, each mechanic sits in a horizontal band coloured by family, positioned at the year it first shipped. A line between two mechanics means the later one derives from the earlier: Raycast Corridor 3D from First-Person Vector Space, Poise and Stagger Break from Stamina Action Economy. Select any node and the graph isolates its ancestry back to a root and its descendants forward to the present. Twelve mechanics have no parent in the data at all. Forty-three have more than one, which is where most of the interesting history sits.

Feature ontology is the primary view: mechanics and the derives links between them. Franchise trees follow titles instead — sequels and softer descent, so Castle Wolfenstein reaches Wolfenstein 3D reaches Doom reaches Quake, and Ultima Underworld reaches System Shock reaches Thief. Studio lineage follows the people and the paperwork: Softdisk to id Software to Ion Storm, Blue Sky Productions renaming itself Looking Glass and then seeding both Irrational and Arkane, DMA Design becoming Rockstar North. Run the same decade through all three and the same events look like an idea, a series, and a corporate restructuring.

Each mechanic carries one origin title, which asserts first notable shipped implementation rather than invention. Derives links assert influence in the loose sense every designer means by it: the later idea is unintelligible without the earlier one. Adopts links mark significant later users and are illustrative, never exhaustive — Object Collision As Verb lists nine adopters and could list six hundred. Nothing here is a claim about intent, and no designer has confirmed any edge. Coverage thins badly after 2020, where the newest entries sit, because a decade is not enough distance to tell a mechanic from a fashion.

home.openingClaim: Genre is a shelving system that hardened into a critical vocabulary. It tells you what a game resembles, not what it is made of, and it collapses under pressure: Dark Souls and Slay the Spire share nothing on the shelf and share a spine underneath, because Bonfire Checkpoint & Currency Risk and Run-Persistent Meta-Progression are both arguments about what death should cost. Mechanics, unlike genres, have parents. Regenerating health in Halo revises hit points in Rogue, which revises collision in Spacewar!, and each step is a specific team solving a specific problem on specific hardware. Almost nothing arrives from nowhere. Of 168 mechanics here, twelve have no traceable parent — Rogue's generated levels, Dune II's real-time production loop, Lode Runner's shipped level editor — and they stand out precisely because descent is otherwise so dense. Tracing that descent explains things genre cannot: why the medium keeps rediscovering the same problems under new names, why an idea can lie dormant for fifteen years and then become load-bearing, and why the honest history of games is a history of arguments between designers rather than a history of console generations.

SPACE.blurb: Twenty-three ideas about where the player is permitted to be, running from a single frame of Pong to a planet you can descend to without a loading screen.
SPACE.essay:
Every entry in this family answers one question: what shape is the space, and what must the player do to cross it. Object Collision As Verb in Spacewar! (1962) is the root of the family and of most of the graph — two things overlap and something happens. Pong compresses that into a Single-Screen Arena, and for most of a decade the frame is the world. Defender breaks the frame in 1980 by decoupling the camera from the playfield, which is the precondition for everything larger than a screen: Super Mario Bros.'s Momentum-Based Platform Control, Metroid's Ability-Gated Interlocked Map, and eventually Grand Theft Auto III's Seamless Streaming Open World, which converts levels into places.

Depth arrives twice. First as a lie — Moon Patrol's parallax layers, Zaxxon's isometric grid, Pole Position's scaling sprites, F-Zero's rotating ground plane — and then as real geometry, in Wolfenstein 3D's raycast corridors and Quake's rooms stacked above rooms. Super Mario 64 supplies the third-person grammar that nearly every 3D action game still runs on.

Designers keep re-litigating one question here: how much of the route belongs to them. Metroid locks space behind capabilities. Assassin's Creed annotates architecture as a climbing grid and calls the result a city. Mirror's Edge makes traversal the primary verb while painting the intended line onto the world. Breath of the Wild deletes the annotation and lets a stamina bar be the only limit. Portal takes the extreme position and hands topology itself to the player. Nobody has settled whether an authored route or an unbounded one makes a world feel larger.

CAM.blurb: Where the eye sits and how intent reaches the character — the two problems the medium solved late, solved badly, and has never stopped revising.
CAM.essay:
Nothing in this family predates 1996, which is the point: while play was flat, the camera was a non-question and input was a switch. Two of the entries here originate in Super Mario 64 alone. Trailing Follow Camera treats the viewpoint as a character with collision and intent. Graded Analog Input ends the era of on/off movement. Both exist because Analog Free-Roam 3D Movement created a problem nobody had needed to solve. Resident Evil answers the same problem in the opposite direction with Fixed Cinematic Camera — pre-authored angles, cheap on hardware and expensive on nerves.

Aiming follows viewing. Ocarina of Time's Contextual Lock-On Targeting fuses camera and combat by letting the system pick what matters. Rainbow Six introduces Iron-Sight Aim-Down-Sights as a mobility-for-accuracy trade. Alien Resurrection ships Dual-Analog Move + Look in 2000 to open ridicule and is now the default posture of the entire medium. kill.switch pins the camera to the shoulder, and Half-Life: Alyx eventually replaces the whole apparatus with the player's own neck.

Running underneath is a fight about ownership. Metal Gear Solid's Directed In-Engine Camera Language argues that the camera is a director's instrument, borrowing cuts and dollies from film. Gran Turismo's Photo Mode argues the opposite — the camera belongs to the player, who is now an audience with a tripod. Nintendogs and Wii Sports both attack the question from beneath by removing the intermediary entirely, making the finger and the arm the input. Every camera decision since 1996 is a position on how much of the frame the player is trusted with.

PROG.blurb: What a game remembers about you between deaths and sessions, from three initials in Asteroids to a battle pass that expires on a schedule.
PROG.essay:
Numeric Score in Pong is the first thing a game ever remembered, and the whole family is downstream of that impulse to keep a number. Space Invaders converts failure into a budget with Lives and Continues; Asteroids writes the number to battery-backed RAM and invents both persistent identity and the leaderboard. Rogue then does two incompatible things in the same year — Experience Points and Levels imports permanent capability from tabletop, and Permadeath Run Structure guarantees you will lose it.

Hardware settles the argument temporarily. Pitfall II's Checkpoint Respawn makes failure a rewind. Metroid encodes state as a password the player carries; The Legend of Zelda's Battery-Backed Save File makes the cartridge remember, which is what makes the modern campaign possible. Diablo's Branching Skill Tree and Colour-Coded Loot Rarity turn progression into a spatial choice with opportunity cost and a one-glance value language, and World of Warcraft compresses that language back into a single ascending number.

Designers argue endlessly about what death should cost. Dark Souls answers with Bonfire Checkpoint & Currency Risk: rest resets the world, death drops your souls where you fell, and you get exactly one attempt to recover them. Rogue Legacy answers with Run-Persistent Meta-Progression, where the run is lost but something survives it — the compromise that made roguelikes mass-market. Call of Duty 4 answers a third way, with Prestige Reset-for-Status, where surrendering everything voluntarily is the reward. All three are grandchildren of the same 1978 decision to charge for another life, and all three are still in active dispute.

NARR.blurb: How fiction is delivered and how much of it the player authors, from Pac-Man's wordless interludes to a story whose subject is your own compliance.
NARR.essay:
Fiction enters the arcade sideways. Pac-Man's Attract-Mode Premise establishes character in vignettes with no interaction at all, and two very different children follow: Dragon's Lair reduces play to a timed prompt over authored spectacle, and Karateka lets the engine take the controller to tell you something. Karateka's In-Engine Cutscene has been contested continuously for forty years and abandoned by nobody.

A second trunk starts with Ultima IV, which ships Branching Dialogue Trees and Explicit Morality Axis together in 1985 — conversation as navigable structure, and a game that scores your ethics. Fallout converts that axis into Faction Reputation, which asks whose side you are on rather than whether you are good, and gets world-state consequences in exchange. Baldur's Gate II gives party members private opinions with Companion Approval, which is why people replay it. Knights of the Old Republic makes accumulated choice reshape the final act instead of a closing slide.

Production values keep raising the stakes and narrowing the options. Night Trap's Full-Motion Video was a commercial dead end that permanently reset expectations; Wing Commander III's Full Voice Performance doubled emotional bandwidth and multiplied the cost of changing a line. Mass Effect's Cinematic Dialogue Wheel is the direct consequence — paraphrased intent, selected radially, so the camera never stops. System Shock had already proposed the cheaper answer, letting the level narrate through Environmental Storytelling and Found Audio Log. BioShock closes the argument by making the player's own obedience the subject, which is the medium doing something no other medium can.

CBT.blurb: Grammar for hitting, blocking, aiming, and dying: sixteen mechanics arguing about what one exchange should cost the player, in time, resources, and nerve.
CBT.essay:
Rogue's Hit Points convert combat from a coin flip into a negotiation, and everything here inherits that premise. Fighting games then supply most of the vocabulary. Street Fighter II's Chained Combo Strings were a bug that survived because they created a skill ceiling nobody had designed; Super Street Fighter II Turbo adds Cancels and Super Meter, a resource earned by fighting well and spent on comebacks; Street Fighter III makes defense aggressive with the Parry and Riposte Window, and Bushido Blade gives attacks and guards geometry.

Shooters develop a parallel grammar. Counter-Strike's Learnable Recoil Patterns make spray deterministic and therefore memorizable, which is the invisible skill curve under competitive play. Halo ships Regenerating Health and Constrained Weapon Loadout in the same 2001 release, replacing the health-pack scavenger hunt with a rhythm of pressure and retreat and turning pickups into decisions. kill.switch makes cover geometry a verb, Gears of War prices a close-quarters kill in vulnerability, and Max Payne makes time itself spendable.

One dispute organizes the whole family: whether recovery should be free. Regenerating health says pressure is temporary and the encounter resets. Demon's Souls says the opposite with Stamina Action Economy, where every swing and every block draws on one shared bar and panic becomes a punishable state, then adds Poise and Stagger Break as a second hidden health bar to force the aggression-versus-patience dilemma. Sekiro takes it further, making deflection rather than distance the core defensive act and converting combat from spacing into rhythm. Two decades on, most action games are still choosing a side.

SIM.blurb: Ten mechanics from the moment a world stops being scripted and starts obeying rules, with all the emergence and all the breakage that implies.
SIM.essay:
Flight Simulator makes the founding commercial argument in 1982: aerodynamics modelled for their own sake, no score attached, simulation itself as the entertainment. Gran Turismo repeats the argument for cars in 1997, modelling tyre load and weight transfer seriously enough that racing games become an equipment hobby. Both descend directly from Spacewar!'s collision primitive, which is the whole family's root.

Visibility arrives with Jurassic Park: Trespasser, whose Ragdoll Physics simulate bodies rather than animating them and become the first widely legible sign that a physics engine is running underneath. Red Faction's Destructible Geometry attacks the designer's assumption of a fixed floor plan, which is precisely why players liked it. Half-Life 2 turns the simulation into a puzzle vocabulary with Rigid-Body Puzzle Physics and then hands the player a Physics Manipulation Tool, one object that teaches an entire system in ten seconds.

Generativity is the reward and the problem. Far Cry 2's Propagating Fire and Fluids spread by wind and terrain, producing hazards no designer scripted and weapons no designer sanctioned. Minecraft's Editable Voxel Terrain proposes the simplest possible world model and gets the most generative one. Breath of the Wild's Systemic Elemental Chemistry makes fire, wind, water, metal, and electricity interact by rule everywhere, which means shipping puzzle solutions nobody enumerated.

Every entry here re-argues the same trade: simulation buys solutions the designer never wrote, and pays for them in guarantees the designer can no longer make. BeamNG.drive's Soft-Body Deformation spends the whole budget on fidelity as spectacle. Breath of the Wild spends it on the player being right in a way the team never anticipated.

WORLD.blurb: Time, weather, ecology, and characters who keep their own schedules — the systems that make a world seem to exist when the player is not looking.
WORLD.essay:
Ultima III's Day/Night Cycle is the first hint that a world runs on its own clock, and almost everything here descends from it. Ultima VII gives characters somewhere to be with NPC Daily Schedules, which converts quest dispensers into a society. Shenmue adds Dynamic Weather that the player cannot predict and the designer cannot stage. Red Dead Redemption 2 fuses both lines into Simulated Ecology, where animals and townspeople have territory, routine, and memory.

A second thread treats the world as pressure. Rogue's Survival Needs Clock — the food clock — makes standing still a losing move without an enemy on screen, and it is the ancestor of the closing circle in battle royale. Ultima Online's Crafting From Gathered Materials gives non-combat play an economy and the world a supply chain, and Minecraft's Free-Form Base Building turns a level into property that outlasts the session.

Generation eventually takes over the staffing problem. Oblivion's Radiant / Generated Activity has the world produce its own incidents, which yields infinite filler and, occasionally, something no writer would have risked. Left 4 Dead's Dynamic AI Director inverts the idea entirely, spawning against the player's emotional state so that difficulty becomes dramaturgy. Shadow of Mordor's Procedural Nemesis Hierarchy is the strongest case anyone has made that character itself can be generated, since the orc who killed you last week comes back promoted and mentions it.

Unresolved throughout: how much fidelity is worth spending on things the player will never notice. Red Dead Redemption 2 answers by spending it anyway, and argues that unwitnessed detail is exactly what produces the feeling of a world.

MP.blurb: Other humans, from two people at one cabinet in 1972 to a hundred strangers matched by rating and a ping system that replaces speech.
MP.essay:
Pong's Same-Screen Two-Player remains undefeated for legibility: one screen, two people, immediate social consequence. Spy vs Spy splits the viewport in 1984 and thereby invents asymmetric information between people sitting on the same couch. Doom's Networked Deathmatch then puts four players on a network with no rules and creates competitive PC gaming, along with a great deal of corporate IT policy. Quake's Internet Client-Server Play supplies the authoritative-server engineering everything after it depends on.

Persistence follows connectivity. Ultima Online's Persistent Shared World is the most ambitious thing the medium has attempted — an economy and a society that continue without you — and its Player Guilds and Clans convert retention into obligation to other people. EverQuest's Coordinated Raid Encounters demand dozens of synchronized players and remain the medium's only real orchestra. Halo 2's Automated Skill Matchmaking then deletes the server browser and makes competitive play a console-scale product, which is the precondition for Call of Duty 4's Persistent Multiplayer Progression, where losing still pays.

Designers keep re-arguing how much other people should be allowed to cost you. Demon's Souls treats multiplayer as weather: bloodstains, scrawled warnings, and sudden hostile invasions you did not opt into. Escape from Tarkov's Extraction Risk/Reward Loop restores real stakes by letting strangers take your equipment permanently. Fortnite's Cross-Platform Play and Apex Legends' Non-Verbal Ping Communication push the other way, lowering the cost of playing with people — one by removing platform walls, the other by removing the need to speak at all, which happens to solve localization, accessibility, and voice harassment in a single feature.

UI.blurb: Maps, markers, journals, and difficulty menus — ten mechanics negotiating how much a game should tell you before play stops being yours.
UI.essay:
Dune II makes information itself contestable with Fog of War, and every scouting layer in strategy descends from it. Doom externalizes spatial memory a year later with the In-Game Automap, which is what makes large levels tractable, and Halo turns that into the Persistent Minimap / Radar, a corner display so useful that competitive players watch it more than the world. Grand Theft Auto III's Waypoint Objective Marker makes open worlds navigable and, in the same stroke, makes exploring them optional.

A quieter thread concerns bookkeeping. Diablo's Spatial Inventory Grid makes carrying capacity a packing puzzle so that leaving something behind is a real decision. Baldur's Gate's Quest Journal has the game track what you were told, which is what permits nonlinear questing without a notepad beside the keyboard.

Contracts with the player form the third thread, and the most contested. Doom's Selectable Difficulty lets players declare their own terms up front, separating access from challenge for the first time. Perfect Dark Zero attaches Platform Achievements to an account rather than a cabinet, rebuilding Asteroids' high-score table as a cross-game identity. Dead Space argues against the whole apparatus with its Diegetic HUD-less Interface — health on the spine, ammo on the gun — treating information as an immersion problem. The Last of Us Part II reframes the argument entirely with its Comprehensive Accessibility Suite, where difficulty is one axis of access among many rather than a single slider, which is the strongest recent answer to a question Doom opened in 1993.

PROC.blurb: Content authored by algorithm rather than by hand: five mechanics that establish scale can be computed rather than stored, and that stories can be outputs.
PROC.essay:
Rogue's Procedurally Generated Levels are the root, and the claim is unusually clean: the dungeon is built at runtime, so nobody has played it, including the people who made it. Infinite content from finite rules, at a moment when storage was the binding constraint. Elite generalizes it four years later with a Seeded Procedural Universe — eight galaxies from a few bytes — and establishes the principle that scale can be computed rather than shipped.

Diablo commercializes the idea by pointing it at items instead of terrain. Procedural Loot Tables combine generated affixes with Colour-Coded Loot Rarity to produce the slot machine at the centre of the action-RPG, and by extension at the centre of Team Fortress 2's Randomized Loot Box a decade later. Generation stops being an answer to memory limits and becomes an answer to retention.

Two late entries push in the opposite direction, toward meaning rather than volume. Dwarf Fortress simulates centuries of Emergent Generated History before the player places a single tile, so that story arrives as a simulation output rather than as authored text. Minecraft's Infinite Chunked World generates ahead of the player forever and turns the seed itself into a social object — a world you can hand to a friend as a string.

Smallest family in the ontology, and the most disproportionate in influence: three of these five are parents to mechanics in other families, from Slay the Spire's run structure to No Man's Sky's planetary streaming to the loot box. Generation is rarely the thing a game is about, and frequently the thing that makes the thing possible.

ECON.blurb: How a game asks to be paid and what that request does to its design, from the quarter slot to a calendar of expiring content.
ECON.essay:
Space Invaders establishes the founding fact with its Coin-Op Difficulty Economy: difficulty tuned to extract another coin, the first time monetization directly authored the difficulty curve. Free-to-play is that arcade model with an unlimited coin slot, which is precisely how the data links MapleStory back to 1978. Everything in this family is a variation on where the payment sits relative to the play.

Wing Commander: The Secret Missions establishes the other trunk in 1990 by selling more of a game you already own, which reframes a game as an ongoing product rather than a finished object. Oblivion's Downloadable Content untethers that from retail and, with horse armour, teaches the industry exactly how small a sellable unit can be. L.A. Noire's Season Pass Bundle then moves revenue ahead of the content's existence, and Destiny's Live-Service Seasonal Content makes the game a schedule, with narrative and economy arriving and expiring on a calendar.

One question runs through all eleven entries: whether the money is permitted to touch the difficulty curve. League of Legends answers no with Cosmetic-Only Monetization, selling identity instead of power, which is the compromise that made free-to-play tolerable to competitive players. Candy Crush Saga answers yes with energy timers and session-length design, and by revenue it represents the dominant form of the medium. Team Fortress 2's Randomized Loot Box is the most profitable and most regulated idea in the industry's commercial history; Dota 2's Seasonal Battle Pass displaced it by trading randomness for obligation. Minecraft's Paid Early Access Development sidesteps the question altogether by merging financing with playtesting.

STLTH.blurb: Enemies that can fail to notice you, and the systems that model failure to notice — seven mechanics that made AI ignorance into a design surface.
STLTH.essay:
Castle Wolfenstein's Line-of-Sight Detection is the founding move and a genuinely strange one: it gives the AI a state of knowledge distinct from the game's. Once an enemy can be wrong about where you are, that wrongness becomes a resource, and every stealth mechanic since has been about shaping it.

1998 is the year the family resolves. Metal Gear Solid ships Graduated Alert States — unaware, suspicious, alerted, searching, resolved — which converts failure from a restart into a recoverable condition, then adds Explicit Detection Feedback so the player can see what the AI knows. Thief takes the opposite approach in the same year. Light-and-Shadow Stealth turns illumination into a measured resource and lighting from art direction into level design; Diegetic 3D Audio Information makes footstep material, distance, and occlusion carry real tactical data, promoting the ear to a primary sensor.

That split is the family's permanent argument: whether the system should be shown or felt. Metal Gear Solid's exclamation point and vision cones make stealth teachable and fair at the cost of admitting it is a machine. Thief's darkness gauge and audible stone floor keep the fiction intact and ask the player to build their own model of what the guard heard. Neither has won; most modern stealth games run both and let a difficulty setting arbitrate.

Ultima Underworld sits slightly apart, contributing Systemic Solution Space — consistent interacting systems in place of authored solutions — which is the immersive sim's founding contract and the reason its descendants keep escaping the stealth genre entirely. Assassin's Creed then moves hiding out of the shadows and into daylight with Social / Crowd Stealth, where behaviour rather than geometry conceals you.

CREATE.blurb: Handing the authoring tools to the player: five mechanics that turn an audience into a labour force, a talent pipeline, and eventually a marketplace.
CREATE.essay:
Lode Runner ships a Bundled Level Editor in 1983, and the premise is fully formed on arrival — the authoring tool is in the box, and the player becomes a designer without asking permission. Everything after it is a question of distribution and ownership rather than capability.

Doom supplies the distribution. Open Data Formats and Mod SDK gave away the WAD format and eventually the source, which created an unpaid apprenticeship pipeline whose graduates produced Counter-Strike, Defense of the Ancients, and PUBG — three of the largest things in the medium, none of them made by the studio that enabled them. Follow the graph's studio lens and the same pattern appears as careers: id Software seeding Ion Storm, Looking Glass seeding Irrational and Arkane.

Roblox closes the loop with a User-Content Marketplace where players build, publish, and are paid inside the platform, converting a game into an economy of games. LittleBigPlanet's In-Game Creation Suite attacks the problem from the other end, making authoring possible with a gamepad and from inside the fiction, so creation is play rather than a separate tool with a separate learning curve. Halo 3's Replay Capture and Sharing extends creation to the act of watching, recording matches as data that can be re-cameraed and clipped — descended, unexpectedly, from Gran Turismo's Photo Mode.

One tension never resolves: who owns what the player makes. Doom's answer was that nobody did, and the results left and founded studios. Roblox's answer is that the platform does, and pays a share. Both answers have produced enormous value, and only one of them has produced it for the people doing the building.

STRAT.blurb: Commanding many things at once, in turns or in real time — five mechanics about whether difficulty should live in the decision or in the execution.
STRAT.essay:
Fire Emblem establishes Turn-Based Grid Tactics in 1990 by combining positioning on a grid with units that level and stay dead, so that consequence is measured in squares and remembered across a campaign. Civilization scales the same logic to millennia a year later with Turn-Based 4X Empire, which is less a game about war than an argument about history delivered as a rules set.

Dune II abandons turns entirely in 1992. Real-Time Base and Unit Production — harvest, build, produce, attack, under continuous pressure — has no parent in this data, which is rare and probably correct: it is one of the medium's few genuine discontinuities. Every real-time strategy game since has been an argument with its template, and two of the largest genres of the following decades emerged from custom maps built on top of that template rather than from studios. Warcraft III's Tower Defense Lane Denial spun a mod into a genre of its own, and Defense of the Ancients, catalogued under Multiplayer, did the same at far greater scale.

What the family keeps re-litigating is where difficulty should live. Real-time strategy puts it substantially in execution — actions per minute, build order, attention split across a map — while turn-based tactics puts it in the decision and lets the player think for as long as they like. Slay the Spire takes the turn-based side to its logical end in 2017 with Deck-Building Run Progression, where the build is assembled during the run, execution is nearly free, and every ounce of difficulty sits in what you chose to pick up.

RHYTHM.blurb: Sound as a mechanic rather than a garnish: five entries on music that reacts to the player and players who must react to music.
RHYTHM.essay:
Monkey Island 2 contributes Adaptive Dynamic Music in 1991, with a score that transitions on the beat to follow player action rather than looping until the scene ends. It has no parent in this data, and it is the only entry in the family where the music is the responsive party. Everything else here inverts the relationship and asks the player to react instead.

PaRappa the Rapper does that in 1996 by judging input against a musical grid, which makes time itself the difficulty axis — a direct descendant, per the graph, of Pong's Numeric Score, since what is being scored is accuracy against a standard. GuitarFreaks adds the Scrolling Note Highway two years later, rendering future input as approaching geometry, and it may be the single most efficient interface the medium has produced: a sight-reading system anyone can learn in ten seconds without instruction. Guitar Hero then attaches a dedicated physical object to that highway, and the Instrument Peripheral makes hardware the entire pitch, which is both why the genre briefly dominated retail and why it collapsed under its own plastic.

Crypt of the NecroDancer proposes the family's most interesting recent argument. Rhythm-Locked Action requires every action — movement, attack, retreat — to land on the beat, fusing a music game with a procedurally generated dungeon crawl so that two genres solve each other's pacing problems. Unresolved across all five: whether music should follow the player or lead them. Monkey Island 2 answers one way, the other four answer the opposite way, and thirty years on, no third position has found much of an audience.

1958-1977.name: Laboratory & coin-op
1958-1977.essay: Four mechanics in this window, and two of them are load-bearing for everything else. Spacewar! contributes Object Collision As Verb in 1962 — two things occupy the same space and something happens — which is the direct ancestor of hit points, combos, ragdolls, destructible walls, and line-of-sight detection. Pong then contributes three at once in 1972: Single-Screen Arena, where the frame is the entire world; Numeric Score, the first thing a game ever remembered about a player; and Same-Screen Two-Player, which remains the most legible multiplayer arrangement anyone has built. Notice what is absent. No persistence beyond the session, no fiction, no camera worth naming, no economy other than the coin. Games in this period are being defined by what the hardware can hold rather than by what anyone wants to say, and the mechanics that survive are the ones cheap enough to compute in real time. Gun Fight, Breakout, Night Driver, and Combat all appear here as adopters rather than originators, refining collision into recognizable forms.

1977-1985.name: The home cartridge
1977-1985.essay: Twenty-six mechanics originate in these eight years, the densest concentration in the dataset relative to the number of games shipping. Space Invaders introduces Lives and Continues alongside the Coin-Op Difficulty Economy, which is the first time monetization directly authored a difficulty curve. Asteroids adds Wraparound Topology and the Persistent High-Score Table. Defender decouples the camera from the playfield with the Continuous Scrolling Playfield, arguably the most consequential spatial idea before 3D, while Battlezone puts the camera inside the world at eye level and Adventure turns the world into a graph of rooms. Rogue alone accounts for five entries in 1980: procedural levels, experience points, permadeath, hit points, and the food clock. Everything the arcade cannot do, the home computer does — Wizardry adds Character Classes, Castle Wolfenstein gives enemies the capacity to fail to see you, Lode Runner ships a level editor in the box, Ultima III starts a clock the player does not control, and Elite computes eight galaxies from a seed. Fiction arrives late and sideways, through Pac-Man's interludes and Dragon's Lair's timed prompts.

1985-1994.name: 8- and 16-bit
1985-1994.essay: Consoles get memory, and memory changes what a game can be about. Metroid's Password Continuation and The Legend of Zelda's Battery-Backed Save File let a game be longer than one sitting, which is what invents the campaign; Metroid's Ability-Gated Interlocked Map makes progression spatial rather than linear. Super Mario Bros. teaches players a physical vocabulary through Momentum-Based Platform Control instead of a binary one. Ultima IV proposes Branching Dialogue Trees and an Explicit Morality Axis in the same release, and Ultima VII gives its characters daily schedules. Street Fighter II's Chained Combo Strings begin as a bug and become a skill ceiling nobody designed. Dune II lands two roots at once — Real-Time Base and Unit Production and Fog of War — neither with a parent in this data. Doom closes the period with four separate entries: Networked Deathmatch, In-Game Automap, Selectable Difficulty, and Open Data Formats and Mod SDK, the last of which turns players into an unpaid apprenticeship pipeline whose graduates ship Counter-Strike and Defense of the Ancients.

1994-2001.name: The 3D rupture
1994-2001.essay: Forty-one mechanics originate here, more than any other period, because 3D invalidated solved problems and forced the medium to re-answer them. Quake supplies true polygonal space and the authoritative client-server model in one release. Super Mario 64 supplies four, among them Analog Free-Roam 3D Movement, Trailing Follow Camera, and Graded Analog Input, and creates the camera problem that Resident Evil answers with fixed angles and Ocarina of Time answers with lock-on targeting. Diablo contributes four, including Branching Skill Tree and Colour-Coded Loot Rarity, and Ultima Online contributes the Persistent Shared World with an economy and a society inside it. 1998 is remarkable on its own: Metal Gear Solid's Graduated Alert States and Explicit Detection Feedback, Thief's Light-and-Shadow Stealth and Diegetic 3D Audio Information, Rainbow Six's iron sights, Baldur's Gate's quest journal, and Trespasser's ragdolls. System Shock had already solved storytelling without cutscenes through Environmental Storytelling and the Found Audio Log, an answer the industry is still using.

2001-2008.name: Broadband & the console shooter
2001-2008.essay: Thirty-seven mechanics, and an unusual number of them are still the default today. Halo: Combat Evolved ships Regenerating Health, Constrained Weapon Loadout, the Persistent Minimap / Radar, and Drop-In Co-op Campaign in one 2001 release; Halo 2 follows with Automated Skill Matchmaking, which deletes the server browser and makes ranked play a console-scale product. Grand Theft Auto III makes the city contiguous with Seamless Streaming Open World and then makes it navigable with the Waypoint Objective Marker. kill.switch introduces Over-the-Shoulder Aim and Snap-to-Cover Combat two years before Resident Evil 4 and Gears of War canonize them. Call of Duty 4 fuses the two lineages with Perk-Based Loadout Customization, Prestige Reset-for-Status, and Persistent Multiplayer Progression, where losing still pays. Elsewhere: Half-Life 2 makes physics a puzzle vocabulary, Nintendogs and Wii Sports remove the intermediary between hand and game, MapleStory imports free-to-play, and BioShock makes the player's compliance the subject of the story.

2008-2015.name: Digital storefronts & indie
2008-2015.essay: Distribution changes who can originate a mechanic, and the origins in this period reflect it. Minecraft accounts for four entries — Editable Voxel Terrain, Free-Form Base Building, Infinite Chunked World, and Paid Early Access Development — from a team that started at one person. Rogue Legacy's Run-Persistent Meta-Progression is the compromise that made roguelikes mass-market by letting the player keep something after losing the run. BeamNG.drive spends everything on Soft-Body Deformation. Meanwhile the largest studios are re-engineering the business model in public: Team Fortress 2's Randomized Loot Box, League of Legends' Cosmetic-Only Monetization, L.A. Noire's Season Pass Bundle, Candy Crush Saga's mobile free-to-play, Dota 2's Seasonal Battle Pass, and Destiny's Live-Service Seasonal Content, which turns the game into a calendar. FromSoftware's contributions bracket the period — Demon's Souls with Stamina Action Economy and Poise and Stagger Break, Dark Souls with Bonfire Checkpoint & Currency Risk — and Left 4 Dead's Dynamic AI Director makes pacing itself a system.

2015-2027.name: Live service & the long tail
2015-2027.essay: Fourteen mechanics originate in this window, and the newest entry in the entire dataset is from 2020, which is a claim about evidence rather than about the industry. Recent origins are synthetic in the precise sense: Breath of the Wild fuses Systemic Climbable Surfaces with Stamina Action Economy to produce Climb-Anything Stamina Traversal, and fuses Far Cry 2's propagating fire with Half-Life 2's rigid bodies to produce Systemic Elemental Chemistry. PUBG combines matchmaking with Rogue's food clock and gets the Shrinking-Circle Battle Royale; Escape from Tarkov adds permadeath to that and gets extraction. Slay the Spire merges a card game with a roguelike run. Sekiro resolves a twenty-year argument between parrying and stamina. Elsewhere, Apex Legends' Non-Verbal Ping Communication and The Last of Us Part II's Comprehensive Accessibility Suite treat access as a design surface, Fortnite drops platform walls, and Half-Life: Alyx restates the camera problem by making it the player's neck.

methodology:
We include a mechanic when it is a discrete, describable thing a game does that other games later did too, and when we can name a title where it first shipped in recognizable form. Cosmetic differences, engine features with no effect on play, and one-off gimmicks with no descendants are excluded. That leaves 168 entries across fifteen families. Families are navigational conveniences — colour and grouping — not taxonomic claims; several mechanics could sit in two of them, and a few sit awkwardly in one.

Origin means first notable shipped implementation, not invention. We assign it to the earliest release we can document where the mechanic is legible as itself rather than as an accident, and we accept that this is partly a judgment call every time. Prototypes, unreleased builds, regional releases, and mainframe software that never shipped commercially all complicate it. Where a mechanic was popularized by a later game, we credit the earlier one and say so: Over-the-Shoulder Aim is dated to kill.switch in 2003, not to Resident Evil 4; Dual-Analog Move + Look to Alien Resurrection in 2000, not to Halo 2.

Parents must predate their children. No feature links to a parent released in the same year or later, and the graph is acyclic by construction. Three link types carry the argument. Derives connects a mechanic to the earlier mechanic it revises, and is the backbone of the feature lens — the claim is that the later idea is unintelligible without the earlier one. Introduces connects a game to the mechanic it originated, one per mechanic. Adopts connects a game to a mechanic it uses significantly without originating; these are illustrative and deliberately incomplete, since a complete adoption list for hit points would include most of the medium.

Known limitations, stated plainly. Coverage is biased toward Western PC and Japanese console releases, because those are the traditions best documented in English. Arcade-era Japan is thin, and several mechanics we credit to home computers likely appeared earlier in cabinets we cannot verify. PC strategy is underweighted relative to its influence, and mobile is represented mainly through business models rather than through interaction design. Twelve entries have no parent, which is more a statement about our sources than about spontaneous invention. Nothing after 2020 is included, since recency makes descent unreadable. Above all, first claims in games history are contested as a matter of routine; treat every origin here as a well-sourced position rather than a settled fact, and tell us when we are wrong.
